newsitem.title: USA: Albright stresses importance of secular Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Albright stresses importance of secular Turkey.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday stressed the importance of NATO ally Turkey remaining a secular state and said she had communicated this message to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

Testifying before Congress, she also said that with the potential accession of Cyprus to the European Union, this was a "time of opportunity" to press for a solution to the dispute on the divided island and she would "use some American influence" to get that process going.
But as in her Senate confirmation hearing three weeks ago, when Albright first signalled her intention to focus anew on Cyprus, she gave no details of what she might be planning.

"The evolution of Turkey is important to us ... It is important for it to continue to be a secular country," she told the House of Representatives Appropriations subcommittee that handles foreign affairs funding.

She said Turkey, as a NATO ally, "is of great importance to us strategically ... and yet there are things going on there which we do not approve of, certainly in the areas of human rights and also generally in terms of their approaches in foreign policy."
In a meeting with Erbakan in Turkey last July, when she was still U.N. ambassador, Albright said, she "made clear that we feel it vital that Turkey remain a secular state."
She was believed to be the highest-ranking U.S. official to have met the Islamic leader, whose Refah party has come to power for the first time in modern Turkish history.

Suspicious of the West, Erbakan has pursued closer ties with Islamic states -- including Iran, which the United States considers a major state sponsor of terrorism -- and is attempting to impose certain Islamic mores on the country.

The administration, which often keeps such criticism private, last month publicly blasted Ankara for threatening military action to stop the Greek Cypriot government from deploying Russian anti-aircraft missiles on the island.

In recent days, U.S. officials privately voiced serious concern about suggestions by Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller that Turkey would block NATO expansion plans if the European Union closes the door to full EU membership for Turkey.

U.S. officials insist they have not been told this is Turkey's official position but they are not happy that an ally seems willing to use NATO expansion plans, a major U.S.-led initiative, as a bargaining chip and are trying hard to paper over any signs of disagreement within the alliance.
As for human rights, the United States said in an annual report issued last month that Turkey had serious rights problems and its record had deteriorated in some ways.

Turkey wants to join the EU but chances are slim because its economy is struggling and its large labour force would flood the job market in Germany and other European countries if Turkish workers were allowed freedom of employment.

The EU, however, has committed itself to begin membership negotiations with Cyprus next year and U.S. officials said if Ankara accepted an agreement on reunifying the island it would give Turkish Cypriots the benefits of EU membership and remove a major obstacle to Turkey's accession as well.

Albright said: "I think there is a time of opportunity now (to negotiate peace on Cyprus) that we need to somehow work on ... I think with the potential accession of Cyprus to the EU it does provide some way of dealing with the problem and we should use that period and we're going to be examining that.
"We have to use some American influence in terms of getting the process moving," she added.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974, when Turkey invaded the island after a coup engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has some 30,000 troops on Cyprus.
